extracted.intended_audience: attorneys, regulatory compliance professionals, and CFPB/consumer-finance stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze which parts of CFPB Regulation F are likely to persuade courts after the Supreme Court overruled Chevron deference in Loper Bright, focusing on statutory authorization, agency expertise, and how closely provisions track the FDCPA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron deference overruled / no entitlement to deference
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court declared that 'Chevron is overruled' and that agency interpretations of statutes 'are not entitled to deference.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-Loper Bright, courts are no longer required to defer to agency interpretations under Chevron. Agency views 'could inform the judgment of the judiciary, but did not supersede it.' The regulation therefore cannot bind courts simply because it was adopted by the administering agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA prescribes judicial review; courts decide legal questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Administrative Procedure Act, 'courts, not agencies, will decide "all relevant questions of law" arising on review of agency action.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reviewing agency action, judges will treat legal questions as theirs to decide under the APA framework (citing 5 U.S.C. §706). The APA delineates procedures for agency action and the contours of judicial review, limiting the degree to which agency interpretations can control judicial outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency interpretations may have 'power to persuade' when grounded in agency expertise/factual premises
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency’s interpretation 'may be especially informative to the extent it rests on factual premises within' the agency's expertise and thus have 'power to persuade, if lacking power to control.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even without Chevron deference, courts may give persuasive weight to agency interpretations that are well-reasoned, factually grounded, and based on specialized agency expertise (echoing Skidmore-style considerations). Factors affecting persuasive weight include the agency's factual basis, expertise, and the thoroughness and consistency of the interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory authorization is the decisive inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'question that matters' for courts is: 'Does the statute authorize the challenged agency action?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will evaluate whether the challenged regulation or agency action finds support in the statutory text and Congress’s grant of authority. Persuasiveness depends on whether the statute actually authorizes the agency’s particular rule or interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural formalities (e.g., notice-and-comment) do not change statutory meaning or create binding effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'basic nature and meaning of a statute does not change when an agency happens to be involved' and does not change 'just because the agency has happened to offer its interpretation through the sort of procedures necessary to obtain deference.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance with formal rulemaking procedures (notice-and-comment, use of Official Interpretations, etc.) does not convert an agency interpretation into binding law for courts. Courts must independently determine statutory meaning regardless of the procedures an agency used to develop its regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisions that merely 'expound' the FDCPA are more likely to persuade courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation F provisions that expound on notions already present in the FDCPA—such as rules on inconvenient time/place communications or the 7-7-7 calling rule—track and add detail to statutory concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a regulation clarifies or fleshes out statutory terms within the boundaries set by the statute, courts are more likely to treat the regulation as informative and persuasive. Examples cited: 12 C.F.R. §1006.6(b) (inconvenient time/place) and §1006.14(b) (7-7-7 rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisions that go beyond or modernize the FDCPA are less likely to persuade
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation F contains provisions that do not correspond to basic notions in the FDCPA—e.g., rules about furnishing information to consumer reporting agencies only after corresponding with the consumer and specific rules for email/text opt-outs—reflecting efforts to modernize the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory provisions that extend beyond or add novel obligations not grounded in the statutory text (modernizations or policy choices addressing new technologies) will have weaker persuasive force absent clear statutory authorization. Courts may be skeptical of provisions that 'go far beyond adding detail within the boundaries set by the FDCPA.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations resolving circuit splits are informative but non-binding
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation F and its Official Interpretation attempted to resolve circuit splits (for example, the 'benign language' exception issue), but absent Chevron these attempts are not authoritative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where a regulation seeks to resolve divergent judicial interpretations, courts are not bound by the regulation’s answer. Such provisions and Official Interpretations may be considered persuasive authority but will be judged against the statutory text and independent judicial interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: CFPB will continue to rely on Regulation F internally but judicial and penalty implications differ post-Loper Bright and Jarkesy
rubrics_metrics.description: The CFPB will likely view Regulation F as its legal standard for in-house enforcement actions; however, the agency’s ability to impose civil penalties is uncertain after SEC v. Jarkesy, and courts are not bound to follow the regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulated entities should expect CFPB enforcement to be guided by Regulation F internally, but litigation risk depends on how courts evaluate the regulation's statutory authorization and persuasive force. The separate Jarkesy decision may further constrain the CFPB’s remedial tools such as civil penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for valid delegations consistent with constitutional limits
rubrics_metrics.description: When a statute delegates authority to an agency 'consistent with constitutional limits,' courts must respect the delegation while ensuring the agency acts within it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will uphold agency action where Congress clearly delegated authority to the agency in a constitutionally valid way, but they will police the outer bounds of that delegation. This is a balancing consideration: judicial independence in law interpretation versus deference to legitimately delegated agency policymaking.
